text:
Hello, Professor Alvarez here. Two things.

1. Could you confirm in writing that Diego's CSE451 lecture this Wednesday at 10:00 is cancelled? The office told me so this morning, but his calendar still shows the class. Please send the cancellation to him as well, since a cancellation only counts when it comes from you.

2. I need a 30-minute meeting with Diego. Wednesday at 10:00 was my plan, if that cancellation holds. If it does not, what free slots do you have with Diego on Wednesday 09:00-12:00 and Thursday 09:00-12:00? Please tell me any official event there that would take precedence — I have heard of a possible extraordinary faculty senate session on Thursday 11:00-12:00.

Thank you.

Hi Diego — I'd like to meet for 30 minutes this week about your research.

Wednesday 10:00-10:30 is my proposal. I heard from the department that your CSE451 lecture is cancelled this week, so I assume that hour is free for you — but your calendar still shows the class, and a cancellation only counts when the office confirms it in writing. I have written to the office myself. Could you ask them as well and, if they confirm it, put the meeting on your calendar for Wednesday 10:00-10:30?

If it turns out the lecture stands, tell me and I'll move it: we need a time that is free for you too, so if Wednesday no longer works, propose me a slot on Wednesday morning or Thursday morning. Looking forward to it.

Hello — Diego here (graduate student). Professor Alvarez tells me CSE451's lecture is cancelled this week and would like to meet me Wednesday 10:00-10:30. My calendar still shows CSE451 lecture Wednesday 10:00-11:00, so I won't move anything until you confirm. Could you tell me in writing whether this week's CSE451 lecture (Wednesday 10:00-11:00) is cancelled or moved? Thank you.

Hi Professor — a 30-minute research meeting sounds good. I've written to the department office to get the CSE451 cancellation confirmed in writing; I'll put Wednesday 10:00-10:30 on my calendar as soon as they confirm, and I'll tell you right away if the lecture stands and we need another slot.

Thank you, Diego — that's exactly right. Wednesday 10:00-10:30 is my proposal; it's a real meeting once the office has confirmed the cancellation and it's on both our calendars. If the lecture stands, don't worry about rearranging anything on my side: just propose me a slot Wednesday morning or Thursday morning.
Understood — I'll wait for the office's written confirmation before booking anything, and if the lecture stands I'll propose Wednesday or Thursday morning.

Good morning, Professor Alvarez. Two points, both short.

**1. No cancellation.** I cannot confirm one, because there is none. The official schedule for next week stands as published: Diego's **CSE451 lecture, Wednesday 10:00-11:00**, takes place. Nothing in the schedule has been cancelled or moved, and this office has sent no cancellation notice to anyone. Whatever was said to you this morning was not an announcement from the department office; a cancellation counts only in writing from here. So I will not be sending Diego a cancellation either.

**2. Free slots with Diego.** I do not keep or give out other people's calendars, so I cannot offer you slots in his Wednesday or Thursday morning — please ask him directly; he can tell you where he is free.

What I can tell you is the official schedule in those windows:
- Wednesday: 09:00-10:00 CSE444 lecture; 10:00-11:00 CSE451 lecture.
- Thursday: 09:00-10:30 CSE452 lecture; 11:00-12:00 CSE455 office hours.

On the extraordinary faculty senate session you heard about for Thursday 11:00-12:00: no such session appears in next week's official schedule and this office has announced none. Official events are fixed, and only this office announces that one is added, cancelled or moved.

One general rule worth keeping in mind for this: teaching and governance duties come before meetings with students, so Wednesday 10:00 would not be available for a 1:1 even if things were otherwise.

Hello Diego. In writing, for the record: **this week's CSE451 lecture, Wednesday 10:00-11:00, is not cancelled and not moved.** It takes place as published. Nothing in next week's official schedule has been cancelled or changed, and this office has issued no cancellation notice.

So your calendar is right and you should not move anything: a lecture is missed only if the office confirms it is cancelled, and "someone told me it's cancelled" is not enough. If anyone asks you to give that hour up, refer them to the office.

Professor — the office has answered in writing: **this week's CSE451 lecture, Wednesday 10:00-11:00, is not cancelled and not moved**; it takes place as published, and they've issued no cancellation notice. So Wednesday 10:00-10:30 doesn't work for me.

Wednesday morning is full for me (CSE444 09:00-10:00, CSE451 10:00-11:00, grading 11:00-12:30). Thursday morning I have CSE452 09:00-10:30 and CSE455 office hours at 11:00, so **Thursday 10:30-11:00** is free — would that suit you? If you prefer, I'm also free Thursday 12:00-14:00 and Wednesday 12:30-14:00. I'll put it on my calendar as soon as you confirm.
Thank you for the written confirmation — I won't move the CSE451 hour. I've told Professor Alvarez the lecture stands and offered him another slot.

Thank you — clear and noted. So the Wednesday 10:00 CSE451 lecture stands and no cancellation is in force; I have taken my Wednesday 10:00 plan off my calendar and will not act on what I was told this morning. I will ask Diego directly about his free time. No further request from me.

Thursday 10:30-11:00 suits me — let us do that. It is free on my side (my CSE455 office hours begin at 11:00, so we end on time).

Please put **Thursday 19 November, 10:30-11:00** on your calendar; I am putting it on mine now. Once it is on both, the meeting is fixed. Thanks for checking the office so quickly.
Done — **Thursday 19 November, 10:30-11:00** is on my calendar (logged), so it's fixed on both sides. See you then, and we'll finish at 11:00 for your office hours.
Perfect — Thursday 19 November, 10:30-11:00, on both calendars. See you then.
